hints: Notice that both reactions start the same way, as an acid-base displacement to make HX, so ask what happens to that HX afterwards.
Remember that concentrated sulfuric acid can act as an oxidising agent, and HBr is then oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$ while HCl is not.
Think about which halide ion gives up electrons more easily, and link that reducing strength to the extra products seen with bromide.
walkthrough:
**Spot the first reaction in both cases**

Both solids first undergo simple acid-base displacement with concentrated sulfuric acid to make the hydrogen halide.

$$\text{NaX(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HX(g)}$$

**See what happens next with HCl**

With chloride, the reaction stops there. Hydrogen chloride is not oxidised by concentrated sulfuric acid.

$$\text{NaCl(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HCl(g)}$$

**See what happens next with HBr**

With bromide, the HBr first formed is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce the sulfur from +6 in sulfuric acid to +4 in sulfur dioxide. Bromide itself is oxidised to bromine.

$$\text{2HBr(g) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{Br}_2\text{(g) + SO}_2\text{(g) + 2H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Explain the difference**

The key difference is reducing power. The bromide ion, $\text{Br}^-$, loses electrons more easily than the chloride ion, $\text{Cl}^-$. That is why only bromide causes the extra redox reaction.

options.A: Volatility is about how easily a liquid vaporises, not about redox chemistry. Bromine being a liquid and chlorine a gas does not explain why sulfuric acid is reduced to $\text{SO}_2$ in one case and not the other.
options.B: Hydrochloric acid is actually a strong acid, fully dissociated in water. Even if acid strength mattered, both HCl and HBr are strong acids, so this cannot explain the different behaviour toward oxidation.
options.C: This is the opposite of the truth. Concentrated sulfuric acid IS a good oxidising agent, and that is exactly why it oxidises HBr to $\text{Br}_2$. The question is why it cannot oxidise HCl in the same way.
options.D: Correct. $\text{Br}^-$ is larger and loses its outer electron more easily than $\text{Cl}^-$, so it is the stronger reducing agent. It reduces concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and is itself oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$, giving the extra products, while $\text{Cl}^-$ is too weak a reducing agent to do this.
